stem: Use this supplied client policy, not unprinted course code. Response R1 has three 20 ms chunks a1,a2,a3: a1 has played, a2/a3 are queued, and its conversation audio extent is 60 ms. On speech-start, cancel R1, clear its queued audio, mark its response ID canceled, and truncate its conversation audio extent to the amount already heard. Then receive late chunk a4 for R1; commit new user turn U2; create R2; receive its 20 ms chunks b1,b2; finally perform one playback step. Canceled-ID chunks are discarded, and each playback step plays one queued chunk. Which final state follows?

options.text: Heard a1 then a2; queue a3,b1,b2; R1 extent 20 ms; U2 retained
Heard a1 then b1; queue b2; R1 extent 20 ms; U2 retained
Heard a1 then a4; queue b1,b2; R1 extent 20 ms; U2 retained
Heard a1 then b1; queue b2; R1 extent 60 ms; U2 retained

assumptions: The sequence and cancellation, queue-clearing, response-ID filtering and audio-extent truncation policies are explicitly supplied; the lecture does not print this state machine.
No playback occurs between the stated events except the final single playback step; the earlier a1 was already heard.
All earlier conversation turns and U2 remain; only R1’s audio extent is truncated. This model does not assert exact transcript-to-audio alignment or a returned truncated text transcript.
Cancellation/truncation succeed in this bounded model. No live API, audio device or course program is executed.

stem: Choose a sustained operating point under this supplied model. Each uncompressed 640×480 RGB-D pair uses 3 RGB bytes plus 2 depth bytes per pixel; audio uses 48,000 bytes/s; the shared transport limit is 40,000,000 bytes/s. A single sequential inference worker takes 80 ms per pair. A nonblocking downstream stage publishes each result 20 ms after inference completes. Every published result must be at most 150 ms old, measured from its capture time. Candidate A captures 30 pairs/s and keeps only the newest waiting pair; B captures 20 pairs/s and keeps every pair FIFO; C captures 20 pairs/s and keeps only the newest waiting pair. Which candidate meets transport, sustained worker and freshness requirements?

options.text: A: newest-only dropping controls age, so the 30 pairs/s transport stream is feasible
C: 20 pairs/s fit the transport; dropping waiting pairs bounds delay while the worker produces 12.5 results/s
B: 20 pairs/s fit the transport, and FIFO preserves all observations without a growing delay

assumptions: All capture streams are periodic, all pairs are transmitted before any dropping, and transport delay/overhead is otherwise excluded.
The worker starts with a new pair at time 0, processes only one pair at a time without preemption, and immediately starts the next available pair.
Newest-only means at most one waiting pair; a new arrival replaces that waiting pair, not the currently processed pair. FIFO has unbounded capacity and drops nothing.
The 20 ms downstream delay does not block or compete with inference. Freshness is checked only when each new result is published, not continuously between results.
All resource values and scheduling policies are supplied educational assumptions, not measurements of the depicted hardware. A candidate must remain feasible for an arbitrarily long run.
